verses.zh: 耶和华的话又临到我说：
verses.en: The Lord’s message came to me:

verses.zh: 「人子啊，主耶和华对以色列地如此说：结局到了，结局到了地的四境！
verses.en: “You, son of man—this is what the Sovereign Lord says to the land of Israel: An end! The end is coming on the four corners of the land![NOTE:1]
notes: Or “earth.” Elsewhere the expression “four corners of the earth” figuratively refers to the whole earth (Isa 11:12).

verses.zh: 现在你的结局已经临到，我必使我的怒气归与你，也必按你的行为审判你，照你一切可憎的事刑罚你。
verses.en: The end is now upon you, and I will release my anger against you. I will judge[NOTE:1] you according to your behavior;[NOTE:2] I will hold you accountable for[NOTE:3] all your abominable practices.
notes: Or “punish” (cf. BDB 1047 s.v. שָׁפַט 3.c).
Heb “ways.”
Heb “I will place on you.”

verses.zh: 我眼必不顾惜你，也不可怜你，却要按你所行的报应你，照你中间可憎的事刑罚你。你就知道我是耶和华。
verses.en: My eye will not pity you; I will not spare[NOTE:1] you.[NOTE:2] For I will hold you responsible for your behavior,[NOTE:3] and you will suffer the consequences of your abominable practices.[NOTE:4] Then you will know that I am the Lord!
notes: The meaning of the Hebrew term is primarily emotional: “to pity,” which in context implies an action, as in being moved by pity in order to spare them from the horror of their punishment.
The pronoun “you” is not in the Hebrew text but is implied.
“I will set your behavior on your head.”
Heb “and your abominable practices will be among you.”

verses.zh: 「主耶和华如此说：有一灾，独有一灾；看哪，临近了！
verses.en: “This is what the Sovereign Lord says: A disaster[NOTE:1]—a one-of-a-kind[NOTE:2] disaster—is coming!
notes: The Hebrew term often refers to moral evil (see Ezek 6:10; 14:22), but in many contexts it refers to calamity or disaster, sometimes as punishment for evil behavior.
So most Hebrew mss; many Hebrew mss read “disaster after disaster” (cf. NAB, NCV, NRSV, NLT).

verses.zh: 结局来了，结局来了，向你兴起。看哪，来到了！
verses.en: An end comes[NOTE:1]—the end comes![NOTE:2] It has awakened against you![NOTE:3] Look, it is coming![NOTE:4]
notes: Or “has come.”
Or “has come.”

With different vowels the verb rendered “it has awakened” would be the noun “the end,” as in “the end is upon you.” The verb would represent a phonetic wordplay. The noun by virtue of repetition would continue to reinforce the idea of the end. Whether verb or noun, this is the only instance to occur with this preposition.

For this entire verse, the LXX has only “the end is come.” tn In each of the three cases of the verb translated with forms of “to come,” the form may either be a participle (“comes/is coming”) or a perfect (“has come”). Either form would indicate that the end is soon to arrive. This last form appears also to be feminine, although “end” is masculine. This shift may be looking ahead to the next verse, whose first noun (“Doom”) is feminine.

verses.zh: 境内的居民哪，所定的灾临到你，时候到了，日子近了，乃是哄嚷并非在山上欢呼的日子。
verses.en: Doom is coming upon you who live in the land! The time is coming, the day[NOTE:1] is near. There are sounds of tumult, not shouts of joy, on the mountains.[NOTE:2]
notes: The day refers to the day of the Lord, a concept which, beginning in Amos 5:18-20, became a common theme in the OT prophetic books. It refers to a time when the Lord intervenes in human affairs as warrior and judge.

The LXX reads “neither tumult nor birth pains.” The LXX varies at many points from the MT in this chapter. The context suggests that one or both of these would be present on a day of judgment, thus favoring the MT. Perhaps more significant is the absence of “the mountains” in the LXX. If the ר (resh) in הָרִים (harim, “the mountains” not “on the mountains”) were a ד (dalet), which is a common letter confusion, then it could be from the same root as the previous word, הֵד (hed), meaning “the day is near—with destruction, not joyful shouting.”

verses.zh: 我快要将我的忿怒倾在你身上，向你成就我怒中所定的，按你的行为审判你，照你一切可憎的事刑罚你。
verses.en: Soon now I will pour out my rage[NOTE:1] on you; I will fully vent my anger against you. I will judge you according to your behavior. I will hold you accountable for all your abominable practices.
notes: The expression “to pour out rage” also occurs in Ezek 9:8; 14:19; 20:8, 13, 21; 22:31; 30:15; 36:18.

verses.zh: 我眼必不顾惜你，也不可怜你，必按你所行的报应你，照你中间可憎的事刑罚你。你就知道击打你的是我耶和华。
verses.en: My eye will not pity you; I will not spare[NOTE:1] you. For your behavior I will hold you accountable,[NOTE:2] and you will suffer the consequences of your abominable practices. Then you will know that it is I, the Lord, who is striking you.[NOTE:3]
notes: The meaning of the Hebrew term is primarily emotional: “to pity,” which in context implies an action, as in being moved by pity in order to spare them from the horror of their punishment.
Heb “According to your behavior I will place on you.”
The MT lacks “you.” It has been added for clarification.

verses.zh: 「看哪，看哪，日子快到了，所定的灾已经发出。杖已经开花，骄傲已经发芽。
verses.en: “Look, the day! Look, it is coming! Doom has gone out! The staff has budded, pride has blossomed!

verses.zh: 强暴兴起，成了罚恶的杖。以色列人，或是他们的群众，或是他们的财宝，无一存留，他们中间也没有得尊荣的。
verses.en: Violence[NOTE:1] has grown into a staff that supports wickedness. Not one of them will be left[NOTE:2]—not from their crowd, not from their wealth, not from their prominence.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “the violence.”
The LXX reads “he will crush the wicked rod without confusion or haste.”tn The verb has been supplied for the Hebrew text to clarify the sense.
The Hebrew word occurs only here in the OT.

verses.zh: 时候到了，日子近了，买主不可欢喜，卖主不可愁烦，因为烈怒已经临到他们众人身上。
verses.en: The time has come; the day has struck! The customer should not rejoice, nor the seller mourn; for divine wrath[NOTE:1] comes against their whole crowd.
notes: Heb “wrath.” Context clarifies that God’s wrath is in view.

verses.zh: 卖主虽然存活，却不能归回再得所卖的，因为这异象关乎他们众人。谁都不得归回，也没有人在他的罪孽中坚立自己。」
verses.en: The customer will no longer pay the seller[NOTE:1] while both parties are alive, for the vision against their whole crowd[NOTE:2] will not be revoked. Each person, for his iniquity,[NOTE:3] will fail to preserve his life.
notes: The translation follows the LXX for the first line of the verse, although the LXX has lost the second line due to homoioteleuton (similar endings of the clauses). The MT reads “The seller will not return to the sale.” This Hebrew reading has been construed as a reference to land redemption, the temporary sale of the use of property, with property rights returned to the seller in the year of Jubilee. But the context has no other indicator that land redemption is in view. If correct, the LXX evidence suggests that one of the cases of “the customer” has been replaced by “the seller” in the MT, perhaps due to hoimoioarcton (similar beginnings of the words).
The Hebrew word refers to the din or noise made by a crowd, and by extension may refer to the crowd itself.

Or “in their punishment.” The phrase “in/for [a person’s] iniquity” occurs fourteen times in Ezekiel: here and in v. 16; 3:18, 19; 4:17; 18:17, 18, 19, 20; 24:23; 33:6, 8, 9; 39:23. The Hebrew word for “iniquity” may also mean the “punishment for iniquity.”

verses.zh: 「他们已经吹角，预备齐全，却无一人出战，因为我的烈怒临到他们众人身上。
verses.en: “They have blown the trumpet and everyone is ready, but no one goes to battle, because my anger is against their whole crowd.[NOTE:1]
notes: The Hebrew word refers to the din or noise made by a crowd, and by extension may refer to the crowd itself.

verses.zh: 在外有刀剑，在内有瘟疫、饥荒；在田野的，必遭刀剑而死；在城中的，必有饥荒、瘟疫吞灭他。
verses.en: The sword is outside; pestilence and famine are inside the house. Whoever is in the open field will die by the sword, and famine and pestilence will consume everyone in the city.

verses.zh: 其中所逃脱的就必逃脱，各人因自己的罪孽在山上发出悲声，好像谷中的鸽子哀鸣。
verses.en: Their survivors will escape to the mountains and become like doves of the valleys;[NOTE:1] all of them will moan—each one for his iniquity.
notes: The simile compares doves that flee their valley home for the mountains, where they coo in mournful discomfort. For doves moaning or mourning see Isa 38:14; 59:11; Ezek 7:16 and Nah 2:7.

verses.zh: 手都发软，膝弱如水。
verses.en: All their hands will hang limp; their knees will be wet with urine.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “their knees will run with water.” The expression probably refers to urination caused by fright, which is how the LXX renders the phrase. More colloquial English would simply be “they will wet their pants,” but as D. I. Block (Ezekiel [NICOT], 1:261, n. 98) notes, the men likely wore skirts which were short enough to expose urine on the knees.

verses.zh: 要用麻布束腰，被战兢所盖；各人脸上羞愧，头上光秃。
verses.en: They will wear sackcloth, terror will cover them; shame will be on all their faces, and all their heads will be shaved bald.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “baldness will be on their heads.”

verses.zh: 他们要将银子抛在街上，金子看如污秽之物。当耶和华发怒的日子，他们的金银不能救他们，不能使心里知足，也不能使肚腹饱满，因为这金银作了他们罪孽的绊脚石。
verses.en: They will discard their silver in the streets, and their gold will be treated like filth.[NOTE:1] Their silver and gold will not be able to deliver them on the day of the Lord’s fury.[NOTE:2] They will not satisfy their hunger or fill their stomachs because their wealth[NOTE:3] was the obstacle leading to their iniquity.[NOTE:4]
notes: The Hebrew term can refer to menstrual impurity. The term also occurs at the end of v. 20.
Cf. Zeph 1:18.
Heb “it.” Apparently the subject is the silver and gold mentioned earlier (see L. C. Allen, Ezekiel [WBC], 1:102).
The “stumbling block of their iniquity” is a unique phrase of the prophet Ezekiel (Ezek 14:3, 4, 7; 18:30; 44:12).

verses.zh: 论到耶和华妆饰华美的殿，他建立得威严，他们却在其中制造可憎可厌的偶像，所以这殿我使他们看如污秽之物。
verses.en: They rendered the beauty of his ornaments into pride,[NOTE:1] and with it they made their abominable images—their detestable idols. Therefore I will render it filthy to them.
notes: The MT reads “he set up the beauty of his ornament as pride.” The verb may be repointed as plural without changing the consonantal text. The Syriac reads “their ornaments” (plural), implying עֶדְיָם (ʿedyam) rather than עֶדְיוֹ (ʿedyo) and meaning “they were proud of their beautiful ornaments.” This understands “ornaments” in the common sense of women’s jewelry, which then was used to make idols. The singular suffix “his ornaments” would refer to using items from the temple treasury to make idols. D. I. Block points out the foreshadowing of Ezek 16:17, which, with Rashi and the Targum, supports the understanding that this is a reference to temple items. See D. I. Block, Ezekiel (NICOT), 1:265.

verses.zh: 我必将这殿交付外邦人为掠物，交付地上的恶人为掳物；他们也必亵渎这殿。
verses.en: I will give it to foreigners as loot, to the world’s wicked ones as plunder, and they will desecrate it.

verses.zh: 我必转脸不顾以色列人，他们亵渎我隐密之所，强盗也必进去亵渎。
verses.en: I will turn my face away from them, and they will desecrate my treasured place.[NOTE:1] Vandals will enter it and desecrate it.[NOTE:2]
notes: My treasured place probably refers to the temple (however, cf. NLT’s “my treasured land”).
Since the pronouns “it” are both feminine, they do not refer to the masculine “my treasured place”; instead they probably refer to Jerusalem or the land, both of which are feminine in Hebrew.

verses.zh: 「要制造锁链；因为这地遍满流血的罪，城邑充满强暴的事，
verses.en: (Make the chain,[NOTE:1] because the land is full of murder[NOTE:2] and the city is full of violence.)
notes: The Hebrew word “the chain” occurs only here in the OT. The reading of the LXX (“and they will make carnage”) seems to imply a Hebrew text of הַבַּתּוֹק (habbattoq, “disorder, slaughter”) instead of הָרַתּוֹק (haratoq, “the chain”). The LXX is also translating the verb as a third person plural future and taking this as the end of the preceding verse. As M. Greenberg (Ezekiel [AB], 1:154) notes, this may refer to a chain for a train of exiles, but “the context does not speak of exile but of the city’s fall. The versions guess desperately, and we can do little better.”
Heb “judgment for blood,” i.e., indictment or accountability for bloodshed. The word for “judgment” does not appear in the similar phrase in 9:9.

verses.zh: 所以我必使列国中最恶的人来占据他们的房屋；我必使强暴人的骄傲止息，他们的圣所都要被亵渎。
verses.en: I will bring the most wicked of the nations, and they will take possession of their houses. I will put an end to the arrogance of the strong, and their sanctuaries[NOTE:1] will be desecrated.
notes: Or “their holy places” (KJV, ASV, NASB, NCV, NRSV).

verses.zh: 毁灭临近了，他们要求平安，却无平安可得。
verses.en: Terror[NOTE:1] is coming! They will seek peace, but find none.
notes: The Hebrew word occurs only here in the OT. It is interpreted based on a Syriac cognate meaning “to bristle or stiffen (in terror).”

verses.zh: 灾害加上灾害，风声接连风声；他们必向先知求异象，但祭司讲的律法、长老设的谋略都必断绝。
verses.en: Disaster after disaster will come, and one rumor after another. They will seek a vision from a prophet; priestly instruction will disappear, along with counsel from the elders.

verses.zh: 君要悲哀，王要披凄凉为衣，国民的手都发颤。我必照他们的行为待他们，按他们应得的审判他们，他们就知道我是耶和华。」
verses.en: The king will mourn and the prince will be clothed with shuddering; the hands of the people of the land will tremble. Based on their behavior I will deal with them, and by their standard of justice[NOTE:1] I will judge them. Then they will know that I am the Lord!”
notes: Heb “and by their judgments.”

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing
is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: EZEKIEL 7:1-4

1Moreover, the word of the Lord came to me saying,
2"And you, son of man, thus says the Lord God to the land of Israel, 'An end! The end is coming on the
four corners of the land. 3Now the end is upon you, and I will send My anger against you; I will judge you according to your ways and bring
all your abominations upon you. 4For My eye will have no pity on you, nor will I spare you, but I will bring your ways upon you, and your
abominations will be among you; then you will know that I am the Lord!'"

7:1 "the word of the Lord came to me saying" As "Lord"
(adon) was so common in chapters 5-6, here, YHWH, cf. vv. 1,2,4,5,9,19,27. This seems to be literary
variety without theological significance (cf. v. 2).

7:2 "son of man" See note at Ezek. 2:1

SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF MAN

▣ "the land (adamah, BDB 9) of Israel" This is parallel to

- "the four corners of the land" (erets, BDB 75, Ezek. 7:2; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY, EARTH)

- "the mountain of Israel," in Ezek. 6:2

- "the wilderness of Diblah/Riblah" of Ezek. 6:14.

This phrase is found only in Ezekiel (17 times, cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 271). It seems to have
the theological emphasis of the Promised Land given by YHWH to His covenant people (cf. Deut. 7:13; 11:9,21;
28:11; 30:20). This special gift, they are about to lose! As God took the Canaanites out of the land because of their evil
(cf. Gen. 15:16), so too, if Israel takes on their ways (i.e. idolatry), He will remove them from the land.

▣ "an end" The time of judgment has come! This word (BDB 893) is used in Ezek. 7:2 (twice),
Ezek. 7:3, Ezek. 7:6 (twice). It is also used in the sense of "climax" in Ezek. 21:25,29; 29:13; 35:5. God
is in control of time and history. His patience and longsuffering are often misunderstood and abused, but
there is a limit!

▣ "the four corners of the land" The word "four" is often associated with the whole earth (i.e.
four directions of the compass, four winds, four corners, cf. Isa. 11:12). Here it is a play on "end." The
end of time is coming to the very ends (corners) of the Promised Land.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #2

7:3-4 Verses 3-4 are repeated exactly in Ezek. 7:8-9. They form a refrain. In many ways this chapter
is a lament (cf. The Prophecy of Ezekiel, by Feinberg, p. 44).

7:3 "I shall judge you according to your ways" This truth is repeated in Ezek. 7:8,9; 18:30; 24:19;
33:20; 36:19; 39:24. Another way to put this recurrent truth is "we reap what we sow" (cf. Job 34:11;
Ps. 28:4; 62:12; Prov. 24:12; Eccl. 12:14; Jer. 17:10; 32:19; Matt. 16:27; 25:31-46; Rom. 2:6; 14:12;
1 Cor. 3:8; 2 Cor. 5:10; Gal. 6:7-10; 2 Tim. 4:14; 1 Pet. 1:17; Rev. 2:23; 20:12; 22:12).

▣ "abominations" This term (BDB 1072) is used in Ezek. 7:3, 4, 9, 20. It is used forty-three
times in Ezekiel, mostly in chapters 7,8,16.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ABOMINATION (OT)

7:4 "For My eye will have no pity on you" See note at Ezek. 5:11. This is repeated in Ezek. 7:9;
8:18; 9:5,10; 24:14. It is a shocking reversal of YHWH's normal character (cf. Exod. 34:6) and acts!

▣ "then you will know that I am the Lord" See note at Ezek. 6:7.
A slightly different form is in Ezek. 7:9. This chapter is like a tapestry of themes woven together to
form recurrent patterns of truth.

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: EZEKIEL 7:5-9

5"Thus says the Lord God,
'A disaster, unique disaster, behold it is coming! 6'An end is coming; the end has come! It has awakened against you; behold, it has
come! 7Your doom has come to you, O inhabitant of the land. The time has come, the day is near-tumult rather than joyful
shouting on the mountains. 8Now I will shortly pour out My wrath on you and spend My anger against you; judge you according to your
ways and bring on you all your abominations. 9My eye will show no pity nor will I spare. I will repay you according to your ways, while your
abominations are in your midst; then you will know that I, the Lord, do the smiting.'"

7:5

NASB, NJB
"a unique disaster"

NKJV, JPSOA
"a singular disaster"

NRSV, Targums
"disaster after disaster"

TEV
"one disaster after another"

REB
"disasters are coming, one after another"

NET
"a one-of-a-kind disaster"

The word "unique" is literally the Hebrew word "one" (BDB 29). Translating it "unique" shows
that there is theological significance to the phrase "one God" (i.e. a unique, one-of-a-kind God). Monotheism is
the stark uniqueness of the OT in its Ancient Near Eastern setting!

The footnote of the Rotherham's Emphasized Bible, p. 790, mentions
that the word "one" is similar to the word "after."

- one ‒ BDB 25, אחד

- after ‒ BDB 29, אחר

The Aramaic Targums translate it "Disaster after disaster."

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

7:6 "It has awakened" The end is personified. It awakens to the activity of judgment (cf. "the sword"
of Zech. 13:7).

The VERB (BDB 884, KB 1098, Hiphil
PERFECT) is also used in Hab. 2:19 in sarcasm of lifeless idols. However,
YHWH is not a lifeless idol; He acts!

Notice the repetition of immediate and appointed time (BDB 773) markers in Ezek. 7:6-12.

- the end is coming, Ezek. 7:6

- the end has come, Ezek. 7:6

- it has come, Ezek. 7:6

- your doom has come to you, Ezek. 7:7

- the time has come, Ezek. 7:7

- the day is near, Ezek. 7:7

- I will shortly pour out My wrath on you, Ezek. 7:8

- Behold the day! Behold, it is coming, Ezek. 7:10

- the time has come, Ezek. 7:12

- the day has arrived, Ezek. 7:12

The VERB
"come" (BDB 97, KB 112, Qal PERFECT) is used eight times in
these verses! This theme of immediacy is repeated in Ezek. 12:23-25,28. Number 6 is a key eschatological
phrase in Amos 5:18-20; Joel; and Zephaniah.

7:7

NASB, NKJV, NRS, NJB, REB
"doom has come"

TEV
"the end is coming"

KJV
"the morning is come"

JPSOA
"the cycle has come"

LXX
"the time is come"

Peshitta
"the dawn. . .is come"

The term (BDB 862, KB 1048, #2) is also used in Ezek. 7:10. It usually means "crown" or "diadem"
(cf. Isa. 28:5). Its meaning in Ezekiel 7:7,10 is uncertain.

- The KJV takes it from an Aramaic root "morning."

- Most English translations take it from an Arabic root, "doom" or "fate."

▣ "tumult" This (BDB 223, KB 552) refers to the panic (originally a divinely given military technique
used against Israel's enemies, cf. Exod. 15:16; 23:27; Deut. 7:23, but also a warning to Israel that if she
was disobedient to the covenant, it would happen to her military, cf. Deut. 28:20) caused by YHWH's coming
in judgment (cf. Zech. 14:13). The judgment referred to is the Neo-Babylonian invasion.

This is not what YHWH desired. He wanted "joyful shouting on the mountains," but His covenant
people forced Him to act in judgment because of their idolatry!

SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC

NASB
"joyful shouting"

NKJV, REB
"rejoicing"

NRSV
"reveling"

TEV
"celebrations"

NJB, JPSOA
"joy"

This term (BDB 212, KB 238) is found only here in the OT. Many assume it is from the root,
"loud noise" (BDB 212), possibly "thunder," which in this context would refer to the sounds of the idolatrous harvest
festivals (cf. Isa. 16:9c; Jer. 48:33).

7:8 "I will pour out My wrath on you" This VERB (BDB 1049, KB 1629,
Qal IMPERFECT) is used several times in Ezekiel (cf. Ezek. 9:8; 14:19;
20:8,13,21; 22:31; 30:15; 36:18). It could have several origins.

- In Ezek. 5:2 it is imagery for "pour out" (BDB 937, KB 1237, Hiphil
IMPERFECT), translated "unsheathe a sword." It may refer to the military
conquest of the Neo-Babylonian military.

- The concept also has a sacrificial connotation of

- "pour out" a libation (i.e. Gen. 35:14)

- "pour out" the life blood at the base of the altar of sacrifice (cf. Exod. 29:12; Lev. 8:15; 9:9)

- "pour out" (same root), used of idolatry in Ezek. 16:15; 23:8

- the opposite of the "pouring out" of the Spirit in Joel 2:28-29 (eschatological)

That which was meant to be imagery for worship and blessing has become imagery for judgment and
destruction!

▣ "according to your ways" See note at Ezek. 7:3.

7:9 "I, the Lord, do the smiting" Normally in the Ancient Near East the
defeat of one nation by another was viewed as the superiority of one national deity above another. YHWH
wants it clearly understood that He uses Neo-Babylon (as He did Assyria, cf. Isa. 10:5) for His purposes.
Israel's defeat is due to their covenant infidelity and idolatries, not His impotence!

John Taylor has a great statement about this phrase in Ezekiel,
Tyndale OT Commentary:

"To hearers and readers who were used to names of God like 'Jehovah-jereh' and 'Jehovah-nissi'
(Gen. 22:14; Ex. 17:15), it must have come home with tremendous force to have Him described as 'Jehovah-makkeh'!
The Lord who had provided and protected was about to strike" (p. 93).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D. #5

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: EZEKIEL 7:10-13

10"'Behold, the day! Behold, it is coming! Your doom
has gone forth; the rod has budded, arrogance has blossomed. 11'Violence has grown into a rod of wickedness. None of them shall
remain, none of their people, none of their wealth, nor anything eminent among them. 12The time has come, the day has arrived. Let
not the buyer rejoice nor the seller mourn; for wrath is against all their multitude. 13Indeed, the seller will not regain what he sold as long as
they both live; for the vision regarding all their multitude will not be averted, nor will any of them maintain his life by his iniquity.'"

7:10-11 Notice the imagery of spring (i.e. budding, Israel's evil has burst into flower).

- "The rod has budded" (note this is where "doom" of Ezek. 7:7 can be understood as "diadem")

- "Arrogance has blossomed"

- Violence has grown into a rod of wickedness

Judah thought her unique position as YHWH's covenant people and the presence of the temple would protect her, even without
obedience and faith! But this false sense of assurance (i.e. #2, arrogance) was about to be clearly rejected! I fear evangelicalism has this same
false sense of security. Conservative theology must issue in Christlikeness, not self-righteousness and judgmentalism. Justification must issue in
sanctification. An initial profession must issue in daily obedience and perseverance (cf. Luke 6:46; Eph. 2:8-10; James 2:14-26). The covenantal
method of being accepted by God has changed from a human-performance basis (OT) to a God-performance basis (NT), but the goal of a righteous
people for the purpose of fellowship with God has not. It is affected by Genesis 3. Now God wants a righteous people to help those who do not yet
know Him to come to Him. The goal has always been Christlikeness! Be careful not to confuse the changing method and the unchanging goal! Also be
careful of a proof-texted assurance connected solely to an initial prayer or rite!

▣ "shame will be on all faces" This was a common idiom for guilt associated with sin
(cf. Jer. 51:51; Obad. 1:10; Micah 7:10). It can be expressed in several ways (see
Interpreter's Dictionary of the Bible, pp. 305-306).

7:19-22 These verses describe Israel's gods.

- money and commerce

- gold and silver idols (cf. Zeph. 1:18)

- YHWH's temple and its wealth have become a boast of pride (cf. Jer. 7), not sanctity and faith

Neo-Babylon will take Israel's collected wealth, individually and corporately.

7:19 "abhorrent thing" This term (BDB 622, KB 673 II, cf. Ezek. 7:20) is used of unclean or impure things or acts.

- menstrual period, cf. Ezek. 18:6; 22:10; 36:17; Lev. 12:2; 15:19-30; 18:19; 20:18

- having sex with a brother's wife, Lev. 20:21

- contact with a corpse (note 6:4-5), Num. 19:9,13,20,21; 31:23

- idolatry, cf. Ezek. 7:19,20; Ezra 9:11; Lam. 1:17

▣ "their silver and gold shall not be able to deliver them" This has two possible meanings.

- Neo-Babylon will not take ransom to spare them (cf. Zeph. 1:18)

- their personal idols of gold and silver cannot deliver them; they are thrown out into the streets

Neither can their wealth or their gods get them food because of the siege!

▣ "an occasion of stumbling" The original meaning of the VERB for
"faith" was a stable stance. The opposite was slipping in the miry clay or stumbling in the way. Therefore,
"stumbling" (BDB 506) is the contrasting concept from faith.

This phrase is literally "for the stumbling block of their iniquity" and is used only in Ezekiel,
but often (cf. Ezek. 14:3,4,7; 18:30; 44:12). The prophet must have coined the phrase. Wealth is not always a
blessing!

in YHWH's name, preached a covenant protection and peace, but there was "no peace" (cf. Ezek. 13:10,16; Isa. 48:22;
